title: General Biochemistry I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L General Biochemistry I curriculum: properties of water, pH and buffers, amino acid structure and acid-base behaviour, protein structure (primary to quaternary) and denaturation, and the classification/structure of carbohydrates and lipids. Bioenergetics, enzymes, vitamins, nucleotide structure and physiological acid-base balance are covered in the continuation course BCH202; detailed metabolic pathways are covered in the 300L metabolism courses.

questions.question: Water's unusually high boiling point relative to other molecules of similar molecular weight is mainly due to?
questions.explanation: The extensive hydrogen-bond network between water molecules requires substantial energy to break, raising the boiling point far above that of comparably sized nonpolar molecules.

questions.question: Water's ability to dissolve ionic compounds and polar molecules is best explained by its?
questions.explanation: Water's polar structure allows it to surround and stabilise ions and polar solutes through electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonds, making it an excellent solvent.

questions.question: What is the pH of a solution with a hydrogen ion concentration of 1 x 10^-4 M?
A solution of pH 3 has how many times the hydrogen ion concentration of a solution of pH 6?
questions.explanation: The pH scale is logarithmic (base 10); a difference of 3 pH units corresponds to a 10^3 = 1000-fold difference in [H+].

questions.question: According to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, a buffer resists pH change most effectively when?
options: The solution pH equals the pKa of the weak acid
The solution pH is two units above the pKa
The concentration of the weak acid is zero
The solution pH equals 7.0 regardless of pKa
questions.correct_answer: The solution pH equals the pKa of the weak acid
questions.explanation: At pH = pKa, the concentrations of conjugate acid and base are equal, giving the buffer its maximum capacity to absorb added acid or base.

questions.question: Which equation relates the pH of a buffer to the pKa of its weak acid and the ratio of conjugate base to acid?
questions.explanation: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), is used to calculate buffer pH.

questions.question: A buffer contains 0.2 M acetate (A-) and 0.1 M acetic acid (HA); the pKa of acetic acid is 4.76. Using log 2 (approximately 0.3), what is the approximate pH?
All 20 standard amino acids found in proteins share which common structural feature?
options: A central alpha-carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom, and a variable R group
A benzene ring in the side chain
A sulfur atom in the backbone
questions.correct_answer: A central alpha-carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom, and a variable R group
questions.explanation: Standard amino acids share this general alpha-amino acid structure; only the R group varies between them.

questions.question: Which amino acid is unique among the standard 20 in lacking a chiral (asymmetric) alpha-carbon?
questions.explanation: Glycine's R group is a hydrogen atom, so its alpha-carbon has two identical substituents (two H atoms) and is not a stereocentre.

questions.question: Which amino acid has a side chain that is positively charged (basic) at physiological pH?
questions.explanation: Lysine's epsilon-amino group has a pKa around 10.5 and remains protonated (positively charged) at physiological pH.

questions.question: Which amino acid's side chain contains an indole ring?
questions.explanation: Tryptophan's side chain is an indole ring fused to a methylene group, distinguishing it from the other aromatic amino acids.

questions.question: Which amino acid contains a thiol (-SH) group in its side chain and can form disulfide bonds?
questions.explanation: Cysteine's side chain thiol group can be oxidised to form a disulfide bond with another cysteine, producing cystine.

questions.question: The isoelectric point (pI) of an amino acid is the pH at which?
options: The amino acid carries no net charge and exists predominantly as a zwitterion
The amino acid is fully protonated on both ends
The amino acid precipitates irreversibly out of solution
Only the carboxyl group is ionised
questions.correct_answer: The amino acid carries no net charge and exists predominantly as a zwitterion
questions.explanation: At the pI, the amino and carboxyl groups are ionised oppositely so that the molecule's net charge is zero.

questions.question: The peptide bond linking two amino acids is formed by a condensation reaction between?
options: The carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, releasing water
Two carboxyl groups, releasing carbon dioxide
The R groups of both amino acids
questions.correct_answer: The carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, releasing water
questions.explanation: Peptide bond formation is a dehydration (condensation) reaction that releases one molecule of water per bond formed.

questions.question: The peptide bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance, which explains why it is?
questions.explanation: Resonance delocalisation between the carbonyl and nitrogen gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character, making it planar and largely non-rotatable, usually in the trans configuration.

questions.question: The primary structure of a protein refers to?
options: The linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds
The folding of the polypeptide into an alpha helix
The association of multiple polypeptide subunits
The overall three-dimensional shape stabilised by disulfide bonds
questions.correct_answer: The linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds
questions.explanation: Primary structure is simply the order of amino acid residues along the polypeptide chain, encoded by the gene sequence.

questions.question: The alpha helix secondary structure of proteins is stabilised primarily by?
options: Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N-H groups within the same strand
Ionic bonds between charged R groups
Hydrophobic interactions between R groups only
questions.correct_answer: Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N-H groups within the same strand
questions.explanation: In an alpha helix, each backbone carbonyl oxygen hydrogen-bonds to the amide hydrogen four residues ahead, stabilising the helical coil.

questions.question: In a beta-pleated sheet, hydrogen bonds form mainly between?
options: Backbone atoms of adjacent, parallel or antiparallel polypeptide strands
Side chains of adjacent residues within the same strand
Only the sulfur atoms of cysteine residues
Only the N- and C-termini of the protein
questions.correct_answer: Backbone atoms of adjacent, parallel or antiparallel polypeptide strands
questions.explanation: Beta sheets are stabilised by inter-strand hydrogen bonds between the backbone carbonyl and amide groups of neighbouring strands.

questions.question: Which bond/interaction provides covalent cross-linking within or between polypeptide chains, formed by oxidation of two cysteine thiol groups?
questions.explanation: Disulfide bonds (cystine) form covalently between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine residues, stabilising tertiary and quaternary structure.

questions.question: Quaternary structure in proteins refers to?
options: The arrangement of two or more separate polypeptide subunits into a functional complex
The sequence of amino acids in a single chain
The local folding pattern of a single polypeptide
The overall three-dimensional shape of a single polypeptide chain
questions.correct_answer: The arrangement of two or more separate polypeptide subunits into a functional complex
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure only applies to proteins with more than one polypeptide subunit, such as haemoglobin's four subunits.

questions.question: Protein denaturation typically involves?
options: Loss of secondary, tertiary and/or quaternary structure without breaking peptide bonds
Complete hydrolysis of all peptide bonds in the chain
Addition of new amino acids to the polypeptide
Formation of new covalent disulfide bonds only
questions.correct_answer: Loss of secondary, tertiary and/or quaternary structure without breaking peptide bonds
questions.explanation: Denaturation disrupts the non-covalent (and sometimes disulfide) interactions that maintain folded structure, while the primary sequence of peptide bonds remains intact.

questions.question: Which of the following is least likely to denature a protein?
questions.explanation: Isotonic saline approximates physiological conditions and does not disrupt protein structure, unlike heat, extreme pH, or heavy metals.

questions.question: Glucose and galactose are both examples of?
questions.explanation: Both glucose and galactose are six-carbon sugars with an aldehyde functional group, making them aldohexoses.

questions.question: Fructose is classified as a?
questions.explanation: Fructose has six carbons and a ketone functional group at carbon 2, making it a ketohexose.

questions.question: Glucose and galactose, which differ only in the spatial configuration at carbon 4, are classified as?
questions.explanation: Epimers are stereoisomers that differ in configuration at only one of several chiral centres; glucose and galactose differ only at C-4.

questions.question: The alpha and beta forms of D-glucose, which differ in configuration at the anomeric carbon (C-1), are known as?
questions.explanation: Anomers are cyclic sugar stereoisomers that differ only in the configuration at the newly formed anomeric carbon created during ring closure.

questions.question: Sucrose is a disaccharide composed of which two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond?
questions.explanation: Sucrose (table sugar) is formed from an alpha-1,2-glycosidic bond between glucose and fructose.

questions.question: Lactose, the principal sugar in milk, is composed of which two monosaccharides?
questions.explanation: Lactose is formed from a beta-1,4-glycosidic bond between galactose and glucose.

questions.question: Which polysaccharide is the primary storage form of glucose in animal liver and skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: Glycogen, a highly branched polymer of glucose, is the main glucose storage polysaccharide in animals.

questions.question: Cellulose cannot be digested by humans, unlike starch, mainly because it contains?
options: Beta-1,4-glycosidic bonds that human digestive enzymes cannot hydrolyse
questions.correct_answer: Beta-1,4-glycosidic bonds that human digestive enzymes cannot hydrolyse
questions.explanation: Human amylases can only cleave alpha-glycosidic bonds; cellulose's beta-1,4 linkages require cellulase, which humans lack.

questions.question: Which class of lipids includes triglycerides and serves primarily as a long-term energy store?
questions.explanation: Triacylglycerols, esters of glycerol and three fatty acids, are the body's main energy-storage lipids, chiefly in adipose tissue.

questions.question: Cholesterol belongs to which class of lipids, characterised by a four-fused-ring (steroid nucleus) structure?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol is a steroid, built on the characteristic four fused carbon rings of the steroid nucleus.

questions.question: A fatty acid denoted 18:2 (omega-6) is best described as?
options: An 18-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid with two double bonds
A 6-carbon fatty acid with two double bonds
An 18-carbon fatty acid with two triple bonds
questions.correct_answer: An 18-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid with two double bonds
questions.explanation: In this shorthand, 18 is the number of carbons and 2 is the number of carbon-carbon double bonds, making it polyunsaturated; omega-6 locates the first double bond from the methyl end.

questions.question: Saturated fatty acids differ from unsaturated fatty acids in that saturated fatty acids?
options: Contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds
Are always shorter than 10 carbons in length
questions.explanation: Saturated fatty acids have single bonds only between carbon atoms, allowing tighter packing than unsaturated fatty acids with double-bond kinks.

questions.question: A triacylglycerol is formed by esterifying one glycerol molecule with?
options: One fatty acid and two phosphate groups
Two fatty acids and one amino acid
questions.explanation: Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups, each of which can be esterified to a fatty acid to form a triacylglycerol.

questions.question: Phospholipids are described as amphipathic molecules because they have?
options: A hydrophilic phosphate-containing head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails
Two hydrophilic heads and no hydrophobic region
questions.correct_answer: A hydrophilic phosphate-containing head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails
questions.explanation: This dual character allows phospholipids to spontaneously form bilayers in aqueous environments, the basis of biological membranes.
